title: Whatsoever things are true (Philippians 4:8)
hookLine: think on whatever is true, modest, just, holy, lovely

lines: A LIST OF THINGS TO THINK ABOUT.
cards: Scroll back through what you looked at yesterday. Not to judge it. Just to notice what filled your head.
The headlines. The arguments. The videos.
The things you checked three times. Whatever gets in, stays a while and moves the furniture around. Paul seems to have known this long before screens.
Near the end of his letter to Philippi, after rejoicing and peace, he gives his friends a list. Not of things to do. Of things to think about.

teach.b: "For the rest, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever modest, whatsoever just, whatsoever holy, whatsoever lovely, whatsoever of good fame, if there be any virtue, if any praise of discipline, think on these things."
Eight items. Some are familiar church words: just, holy. But others sound less like church and more like the Greek philosophers' schools.
Virtue, aretē, was one of their great words: excellence. Lovely means lovable, winning, the kind of thing people are drawn to. Of good fame means well spoken of.
Paul is reaching into the best of the wider culture and saying: that too. Whatever is true, wherever you find it. Then the verb: think on these things.
The Greek word is logizesthe, a counting word, used for reckoning accounts.
Take stock of these. Add them up. Dwell on them on purpose.
Christian thinkers took this openness seriously.
Justin Martyr wrote that whatever had been rightly said by anyone belongs to Christians. Centuries later, Thomas Aquinas read Aristotle with great care.

And Paul ties the list to a promise in the next verse: do the things you've learned and seen, and the God of peace will be with you. This isn't about ignoring the hard news. Paul is in prison while he writes it.
It's about choosing what you let settle in the mind, and what you leave at the door.

how: Catholic spiritual writers encourage guarding the imagination and filling the mind with good things through spiritual reading, sacred art and music; Philippians 4:8 is often quoted in that advice.

games.q: you're Paul, writing to friends who live in a pagan city full of philosophers. what do you say about the good things in their culture?
o: whatever is true, just, lovely, think on these things.
only scripture is worth thinking about.
games.why: "whatsoever things are true... if there be any virtue... think on these things." he even uses the philosophers' word for virtue.

practice: Choose one thing from Paul's list: something true you learned recently, something just you saw someone do, something lovely, a face, a song, the light this morning.

Hold it in your mind on purpose, and when your thoughts drift to a worry or an argument, gently bring them back and turn the good thing over. If you pray, thank God for it; if not, let it stay and take up room.

wordCard.voice: Arete, excellence. Paul's list of eight things worth thinking about: true, modest, just, holy, lovely, of good fame, virtue, praise. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: virtue, excellence; a word of the philosophers' schools, in Philippians 4:8.
